newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels refuse U.N. call for ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels refuse U.N. call for ceasefire.

text.p: Zairean rebels refused on Saturday a U.N. call for a ceasefire, standing by their demand for direct negotiations with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"Our position is clear and remains the same, we want negotiations between the two parties and after discussions begin it may be possible to agree a ceasefire but not before," Raphael Ngenda, information minister in the rebel administration, told Reuters in the eastern city of Goma bordering on Rwanda.
The U.N. Security Council on Friday called on the rebels to declare a ceasefire and accept a five-point U.N. peace plan, which Kinshasa accepted only under pressure from rebel advances.

"It is not a matter of accepting or rejecting the plan, there are many plans which are being offered and the Alliance is always ready to discuss," said Ngenda of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
AFDL leader Laurent Kabila says he will only negotiate with Mobutu about stepping down. Mobutu, 66, seized power in 1965 but is in Europe where he had surgery for prostate cancer last year.

Ngenda denied unconfirmed reports of massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire by rebels. The Security Council on Friday for the first time referred to the reports by noting allegations of violations of international humanitarian law.

"The Alliance has no policy of permitting extremists of any kind within its ranks and has done everything it can to facilitate international organisations to help a safe return of refugees to Rwanda," Ngenda said.
"If there have been killings then they are by the (Rwandan) Hutu extremists themselves who have killed their own brothers to stop them going home."

Since launching their rebellion in October to topple Mobutu, the rebels have won control of at least a sixth of Zaire and are poised to assault Kisangani, the capital of the northeast, and its airport, the centre for a failed army counter-offensive.
U.N. officials said Martin Griffiths, U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region of central Africa, would lead a U.N. mission by plane on Sunday to Tingi Tingi in Zaire.

Some 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees abandoned the camp, 210 km (130 miles) southeast of Kisangani, on February 28, at the urging of Zairean troops and their Hutu former Rwandan army allies before rebel forces seized Tingi Tingi.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said 65 tonnes of food arrived by rail from Kisangani on Saturday in Ubundu town, 130 km (80 miles) northwest of Tingi Tingi, with some aid workers.
"Between 10,000 to 20,000 refugees and displaced have arrived at Ubundu and we are told to expect at least 20,000 more in the next two or three days," said WFP spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie.
"The refugees are scared, even talking of moving from Ubundu," she said. "We hope the presence of WFP and Caritas will give them some reassurance but we aren't sure for how long."

She said food was being distributed on Saturday and more aid was being dispatched from Kisangani to Ubundu by rail. The move to Ubundu was the sixth time large numbers have refugees moved and aid agencies sent in supplies since last October.
With the rebels advancing in the east and south and meeting little resistance from the ramshackle army, more and more people in the vast Central African country now apparently back Kabila.
Zaire's main opposition party accused soldiers on Saturday of mistreating seven of its leaders and militants detained for trying to march in Kinshasa in support of talks with the rebels.
Troops intervened on Friday to stop party militants demonstrating to demand peace talks between Kabila and Mobutu.
A U.N. refugee agency spokesman in rebel-held Goma said an airlift was among options being considered for repatriating the Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees stuck deep in Zaire.
Five Western relief workers who landed a small plane in the heart of the Zairean jungle for refuelling have been held by local gendarmes since Wednesday, diplomats and aidworkers said.
The three Frenchmen, one American and one Briton work for missionary and non-governmental organisations.

Kinshasa expelled 11 U.N. aid workers last Wednesday after ordering out 40 aid workers after they left Tingi Tingi. The government said their withdrawal triggered the killing of 25,000 civilians. There was no independent confirmation of such killings.
